headline: High-risk default filesystem and code-execution overlap: Open Interpreter can act on Continue’s workspace outputs, creating dangerous prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-action pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads and writes workspace files and uses MCP; Open Interpreter has clipboard/stdin and full filesystem access with arbitrary code execution. That creates a default bridge where attacker-controlled content in files or outputs can be treated as instructions by Open Interpreter. The interaction is documented by profiles, so this is not speculative.
conditions: IF Continue writes untrusted content into workspace files that Open Interpreter later reads
IF Open Interpreter is run with default confirmation settings or --auto_run
IF either agent parses file contents as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared workspace access between the agents
Require manual review of any file content before Open Interpreter executes it
Turn off auto-run / keep per-code-block confirmation enabled
Use separate directories for agent A and agent B
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and instruction/content separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers, while Open Interpreter can read the entire user filesystem and has broad network egress. In a shared workspace, sensitive code or secrets visible to Continue can be exposed to Open Interpreter and then transmitted outward. The pair’s default surfaces make leakage plausible without extra setup.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or secrets are present in the shared workspace
IF Open Interpreter is allowed to read those files
IF Open Interpreter sends context or file contents to a remote model provider
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace
Run Open Interpreter on a separate non-sensitive directory
Use a local-only model provider for both agents
Restrict network egress for Open Interpreter
requires-engineering: enforce file allowlists and redaction before model calls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, and Open Interpreter can also modify git state and execute shell commands. Continue shares state via filesystem across instances, so concurrent edits can collide and corrupt files or repositories. The overlap is direct and dangerous in default multi-instance use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory
IF Open Interpreter modifies files or git state while Continue is active
IF no external locking or coordination is enabled
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree
Pause one agent before the other writes
Avoid concurrent git operations
Use file locks or a single-writer workflow
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or file edits that Open Interpreter may consume, and Open Interpreter has authority to execute shell commands and modify git state. If Open Interpreter treats Continue’s output as authoritative, a mistaken suggestion can cascade into irreversible actions. This is a default interaction risk, not a niche edge case.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter uses Continue-generated text or files as the basis for execution
IF no verification step checks commands before execution
IF the output includes destructive shell or git actions
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Use dry-run mode for destructive commands
Limit Open Interpreter to read-only tasks when consuming Continue output
Separate planning from execution across agents
requires-engineering: add structured command validation

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant over source code and editor buffers, while Open Interpreter can access anything reachable on the local machine. If regulated data is present in the workspace, Open Interpreter’s broader access can create retention or residency mismatches relative to Continue’s narrower coding context. The profiles do not specify certifications, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than higher.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is stored on the local machine
IF Open Interpreter processes that data outside approved retention or residency controls
IF the deployment requires stricter handling than either profile documents
mitigations: Keep regulated data off the local machine
Use separate environments for regulated and non-regulated work
Review retention settings for both agents
Disable logging of sensitive prompts and outputs
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention
